text: Six ideas follow from that, and the sections below teach each one: In Python In C++ Why C++ does it this way Section You run the source file A compiler turns each .cpp file into machine code, then a linker joins the pieces into one program Machine code runs without an interpreter, so loops cost nanoseconds, not tens of nanoseconds 1 b = a makes a second name for the same object auto b = a; makes a copy ; you ask for a reference ( & ) or a pointer ( * ) explicitly Values sit inline in memory, with no per-object header or reference count 2 Every object lives on the heap until the last reference goes Local variables live on the stack and die at the closing brace; you choose the heap when you need it The stack is free to allocate and free 3 with open(...) for cleanup RAII : every object's destructor runs at a known moment, so every resource is released by one Deterministic cleanup with no garbage collector 4 , 5 Assignment never copies a big object Move semantics : a value can hand its heap buffer to another instead of being copied Copy by default would otherwise make returning a vector expensive 6 Bugs raise exceptions Many bugs are undefined behaviour : no error, the program means nothing, and the optimiser may make it do anything Checking every index and every overflow would cost speed; C++ checks only when you ask 12 The rest (classes, templates, the standard library, lambdas, error handling) is the toolkit you write with; sections 7 to 11 teach it with the problem each feature solves, what it costs, and the usual mistakes.
